headline: High-risk pair: shared browser/MCP and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can run browsers and use MCP, so a shared content channel is plausible. next-ai-draw-io ingests PDFs, text, images, and diagrams, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks; that combination can let attacker-controlled content flow into instruction parsing. No provenance isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF either agent ingests untrusted web or document content through browser output or MCP messages
IF the orchestrator forwards one agent's raw output into the other's tool prompts without provenance tags
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of browser-rendered content into prompts
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent messages
Restrict MCP servers to allowlisted tools only
Review prompt templates for instruction-following from file content
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance filtering at the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: next-ai-draw-io handles API keys and broad network egress, while oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, and provider authentication data. If they share a workspace or credentials store, sensitive material can flow from one agent into the other's outputs or third-party APIs. The profiles do not document isolation strong enough to rule this out.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace, config directory, or credential store
IF either agent forwards its context to external model APIs during normal operation
mitigations: Separate workspaces and config directories per agent
Remove secrets from shared files before running either agent
Disable network egress for one agent during sensitive tasks
Rotate any API keys exposed to shared contexts
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret scoping and egress policy

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents support multiple instances and broad network egress, and oh-my-openagent can spawn subprocesses while next-ai-draw-io uses browser and MCP-driven workflows. That creates overlapping write and execution pressure on shared resources if they are co-located, though the profiles do not prove unrestricted shared filesystem writes. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents are launched against the same mutable workspace or config tree
IF either agent writes generated artifacts while the other edits or renames files in place
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate directory
Serialize file edits with a simple lock file
Avoid concurrent runs on the same repository
Snapshot the workspace before agent execution
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: oh-my-openagent exposes task and message actions, so it can operationalize upstream outputs, while next-ai-draw-io produces AI-assisted visualizations from documents and diagrams. If B treats A's generated content as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream tasks or messages. No verification step is documented, so the safer high severity is warranted.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent uses next-ai-draw-io output as task input or message content
IF the downstream workflow executes actions without human verification
mitigations: Require human review before task creation or sending messages
Add a verification step for all A-to-B handoffs
Mark A outputs as untrusted in B prompts
Limit B to drafting only, not executing
requires-engineering: implement structured validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: next-ai-draw-io handles API keys and document content, while oh-my-openagent handles provider authentication data, session history, and project code. If either agent processes regulated or residency-bound data, their documented broad egress and third-party API use can create retention or jurisdiction mismatches. The profiles do not specify a single regulated class, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data or residency-bound documents are processed by either agent
IF logs or session history are retained by one agent longer than the other
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data to either agent
Review retention settings for logs and session history
Use separate tenants or accounts for each agent
Document data-flow boundaries before deployment
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
